37.21.0.en: 32- The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him.

37.21.1.en: 33- The LORD will not leave him in his hand, nor condemn him when he is judged.

37.21.2.en: 1- The wicked man uses his authority in this age to wrong the righteous, because the wicked man is full of evil, and because the light in the life of the righteous exposes the wicked man's evil.

37.21.3.en: 2- The wicked man watches the righteous not to learn from him, but to wrong him, because evil has blinded the wicked man's eyes, so that he wants to get rid of the righteous.

37.21.4.en: 3- God intervenes to rescue the righteous from the hand of the wicked, however great the wicked man's power, as He delivered David from the hand of Saul, Mordecai from the hand of Haman, and chaste Susanna from the hands of the two elders (Dan 13). In some cases God wants to give the righteous a greater crown, so he endures the wicked man's wrongs throughout his life, and God does not leave him, but gives him greater glory in the Kingdom of Heaven, in addition to consolations, peace and joy on earth.

37.21.5.en: 4- When the righteous stands before God on the Day of Judgment he is not condemned or judged; first because he is repentant of his sins. And second, God disregards the false accusations that the wicked man directed at him in life, for they are void in God's sight, and on the contrary He compensates him for his endurance of the wicked man with great blessings in heaven.

37.21.6.en: 5- The scribes and Pharisees tried to destroy Christ many times, and they used to watch Him to catch Him in some fault; this prophecy applies to Him, and He said to Pilate, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (Jn 19:11).

37.22.0.en: 34- Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he shall exalt thee to inherit the land: thou shalt look on till the wicked are cut off.

37.22.1.en: 1- In the end this part tells us about God's protection of His righteous children; God calls His children to wait for Him and keep His way, that is, to hold fast to His commandments and walk uprightly, and not to be troubled by the cruelty of the wicked and their domination, because it is temporary and passing.

37.22.2.en: 2- God declares the reward of the righteous, which is their being lifted up to heaven, to dwell in the new earth, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, to receive rest and blessing in place of all that they endured on earth.

37.22.3.en: 3- To this reward is added that the righteous see with their eyes the passing away of the glory of the wicked, and even their separation from God and their being cast into hell. And these rewards are a divine gift from God, who lifts them up and gives them in heaven what surpasses the mind.

37.22.4.en: Hold fast to God's commandments and do not doubt God's way, however much you see the success of the wicked, but pray for them, that perhaps they may repent.

37.23.s.en: (4) The punishment of the wicked and the reward of the righteous

37.23.0.en: 35- I have seen the wicked mighty, and spreading like a flourishing, fresh tree.

37.23.1.en: 36- He passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found.

37.23.3.en: Spreading: describing a tree that extends, with many branches and leaves and wide shade. Flourishing: a tree that grows in its native land and by the courses of rivers. It is a natural tree that grows strongly in its original soil.

37.23.5.en: 1- The wicked man becomes great in much glory on earth as a mighty man, and has great authority like the spreading tree that overshadows others, but all this is temporary, and ends quickly during his life on earth, that is, his condition changes, and he loses his greatness and becomes lowly, as happened with Nebuchadnezzar the great king of Babylon when he was driven from his kingdom and lived like the animals. His greatness on earth may extend throughout his life, but torment will be his in eternity, and he will not be in God's presence.

37.23.6.en: 2- The wicked man appears strong like the tree that grows in its native land, drinks from the waters of the rivers near it and is full of vitality, but all this is outward, because within the wicked man there is turmoil; he has lost his peace despite his outward glory.

37.23.7.en: 3- The life of the wicked man, if measured against eternity, is nothing, and is like a person who passed quickly and disappeared; he is worthless before God, though he dazzled the people around him in his life on earth, but he has no existence before God, because he did not know God, nor did he live purely, nor did he do good. Likewise the righteous pays no attention to the wicked man, however great his glory, for he sees his wicked deeds that neither build up nor benefit.

37.23.8.en: 4- Whoever is proud and exalts himself, his life ends quickly and his weakness appears, like the Pharaoh of Egypt in the days of Moses, who was proud against God, so God struck him with the ten plagues, and then he was drowned in the sea.

37.24.0.en: 37- Observe the perfect and behold the upright: for the end of the man of peace.

37.24.1.en: 38- But the wicked shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off.

37.24.3.en: 1- David calls for observing the righteous man who walks in perfection and uprightness, for he lives with God, and his life is an example to those around him, and he deserves that others be discipled at his hands.

37.24.4.en: 2- The end of a person shows the nature of his life and conduct; the righteous who enjoyed peace and made peace in all his steps, his end is eternal happiness in the Kingdom. But the wicked who was immersed in his evils perishes, and God destroys him and casts him into eternal torment, and he enjoys nothing of the glories of the Kingdom.

37.25.0.en: 39- But the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD: he is their stronghold in the time of trouble. 40- And the LORD shall help them and deliver them: he shall rescue them from the wicked and save them, because they trust in him.

37.25.1.en: 1- Although the righteous are exposed to many afflictions, and this appears in front of the wicked, God intervenes by His power and grace, and saves them; therefore they are at rest however much the wicked surround them, because God cares for them and saves them.

37.25.2.en: 2- The salvation of the wicked [sic] is not meant to be salvation from material afflictions, for these are the lesser matter, but rather salvation from sin and the devil's plots, for God delivers them as long as they take refuge in Him.

37.25.3.en: 3- God's protection of the righteous is like a stronghold that cannot be stormed; it is constant and strong protection, and therefore the righteous enjoy inward peace.

37.25.4.en: 4- The time of trouble is the time of falling into sin, so the righteous takes refuge in God and He delivers him from it, and if he falls he repents, and God returns him to His embrace.

37.25.5.en: And the time of trouble is our life in the world, where we meet afflictions, but God delivers His children from them and turns them to their good.

37.25.6.en: And in the end the time of trouble is the Day of Judgment, when God becomes a stronghold for His children, takes them to the Kingdom, and protects them from the authority of the devil. But the wicked go to eternal torment.

37.25.7.en: 5- Though afflictions exist in this world and the wicked surround the righteous, God becomes a stronghold for His children throughout life until He takes them to the Kingdom, while the wicked are sent to destruction, like the wheat and the tares that grow together, and the wheat is gathered into the barns, but the tares are burned with fire (Mt 13:30).

37.25.8.en: Take refuge in God with confidence in all your afflictions, and in all the wars of the devil with which he fights you, for He is able to deliver you however great your weakness, and to protect you however much threats surround you.

37.25.9.en: Repentance and the seeking of salvation. "O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

37.25.10.en: 1- Its author: David the prophet, as the title of the psalm states.

37.25.12.en: After David's fall into the sin of adultery with Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and after the killing of his son Amnon for his adultery with his sister Tamar, and after his son Absalom rose up against him and drove him out of the kingdom. Some think that he was also struck with a bodily illness; all this reminded him of his sin, so he wrote this psalm full of feelings of repentance.

37.25.13.en: 3- This psalm shows us the hideousness of sin and its effects, so that we hate it and Satan does not catch us with its temporary pleasure.

37.25.14.en: 4- Although this psalm carries many sufferings, and the Fathers count it a lament of David, it ends with hope.

37.25.15.en: 5- This psalm is liturgical; it used to be repeated with the offering of the oblation, with which incense was also placed and burned on the altar (Lev 2:2); it reminds the one presenting the offering of his sins and their effects so that he may repent of them. The Ashkenazi Jews (those from Eastern Europe) used to pray it on the evening of the third day of every week.

37.25.16.en: It was also prayed in the second century before Christ, in the days of King Antiochus, for the whole nation of the Jews on the Sabbath, and therefore we find in the title of this psalm in the Septuagint "for a remembrance, concerning the Sabbath."

37.25.17.en: The Sabbath is the day of rest which signifies eternity, and this psalm is a reminder of sin as a preparation for eternity, for eternity cannot be reached without repentance.

37.25.18.en: And when we pray with this psalm and praise God we ourselves become a sacrifice of love before God, that is, we ourselves become a remembrance before God that gladdens His heart.

37.25.19.en: 6- This is the third of the seven penitential psalms, which are, as we mentioned, (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).

37.25.20.en: 7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms because it contains many verses that signify Christ (v. 6, vv. 11-14).

37.25.21.en: 8- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

38.0.0.en: 1- O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure. 2- For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore.

38.0.3.en: 1- David does not refuse God's rebuke or chastening, but implores God's tenderness and love, that the chastening and rebuke not be in wrath; for who can bear God's wrath?

38.0.4.en: 2- Though I deserve punishment for my sins, yet rebuke me first, and give me an opportunity to repent before You are angry with me, O Lord, and punish me; for the punishment of sin is destruction. But rebuke and chastening lead to repentance and return to You and life with You.

38.0.5.en: 3- This is the beginning of the sixth psalm, which is a psalm of repentance, so there is a similarity between the two psalms in meaning.

38.0.6.en: 4- David felt that the words of Nathan the prophet, whom God sent to him to rebuke him for his sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, were strong in their effects on him, so that he likened them to the arrows that stuck fast in him, and to God's strong hand that came down and pressed on him. This shows that David, despite his fall into sin, loves God and is greatly moved by His words.

38.0.7.en: 5- God's arrows that stuck fast in David may be the bodily and psychological pains that struck him when Nathan rebuked him, and they resemble the bodily pains that struck Job to call him to repentance, and Job called them the arrows of the Almighty (Job 6:4).

38.0.8.en: 6- The coming down of God's hand upon David is divine pressure to lead him to repentance, and at the same time it is help to assist him in repenting, and to protect him from despair, and also from laxity; it is the hand of God the tender Father who wants his salvation.

38.0.9.en: 7- God's arrows indicate God's promises, for Nathan told David, when he confessed his sin, that the Lord had put it away from him (2 Sam 12:13). So God's arrows are strong promises that stuck fast in David's heart, and gave him a hope mingled with the tears of repentance.

38.0.10.en: 8- These arrows signify Christ's love, which was offered on the Cross; it sticks fast in the heart of every sinner to wound him, so that he is moved and returns by repentance to God. And so he receives forgiveness of his sins. Christ is the Father's arrow that caught us sinners and brought us back to life in Him.

38.1.0.en: 3- There is no health in my flesh because of thine anger; there is no soundness in my bones because of my sin.

38.1.1.en: 1- When David felt God's anger against him because of his sin he was greatly affected spiritually, psychologically and also bodily, because he fears God and loves Him, so he felt the guilt of his sin, and his health was affected, so he was in bodily weakness. He declares his humbling before God, his humility and his repentance of his sin.

38.1.2.en: 2- By David's bones is meant his inside, for the bones are the deepest thing in man's body, and they support the body and give it form; that is, David's inward being, his mind and his feelings and all that is in him was greatly affected, and even lost its inward peace because of his sin, so he declares his need of God, that He may forgive him and restore his peace to him.

38.1.3.en: 3- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, and in it He speaks of His sufferings that He endured because of our sins, for He bore in His body on the Cross the consequences of the whole world, and suffered and died to redeem us.

38.1.4.en: 4- This verse shows the hideousness of sin, which shakes man's being; David, who was not terrified by the lion and the bear that he killed, nor by Goliath whose head he cut off, was greatly disturbed as a result of his fall into sin.

38.2.0.en: 4- For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me.

38.2.2.en: 1- David reflected on his sins and found that they were many; for though he had fallen into adultery and murder, he thought that his sins had many effects. He caused the wife of Uriah to stumble and fall, and likewise his sin was a betrayal of his wives, in addition to the fact that he sinned against God and against his own body, and also became a bad example to Joab the commander of his army, and to many around him who knew of the matter, and he wronged one of the commanders of his army, who was Uriah, and also caused Joab to stumble and made him share with him in killing Uriah, and betrayed his army that fought for him ... so he felt that he had not sinned two sins only, but many sins had risen over his head and covered his whole being. He is truly a man repentant with all his heart, who knows how to judge himself.

38.2.3.en: 2- Sin, which seems sweet in its moment, presses upon man, pricks his conscience and affects his whole being. The wise man guards against any sin however attractive it is.

38.2.4.en: 3- The humble man bows his head, so he does not grow weary under the weight of sins, but God has mercy on him and lifts them from him. But the proud man feels their weight upon him and cannot bear it.

38.2.5.en: 4- When the iniquities covered David's head, that is, the thoughts of sin, they took away his discernment and understanding, so he was led without understanding and fell into sin; therefore beware of haste in any action, lest lust drive us into many sins.

38.3.0.en: 5- My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness.

38.3.2.en: Wounds: a wound that has not healed.

38.3.3.en: 1- David feels that his sin affected him like a disease that produced wounds and pus, and some think that a bodily disease actually struck him after his sin, but here he speaks rather of the effects of his sin; that they are like wounds and pus that wearied his body so that he suffered bodily, in addition to the psychological and spiritual pains.

38.3.4.en: 2- Sin is the result of foolishness and stupidity; it appears in the sinner's sight as pleasure and gain, but its reality is the demolition and destruction of man. But when he repents he understands all this; David at the hour of his sin saw that his sin was right, but when he repented he felt its hideousness and that it was a stench, a wound and folly.

38.3.5.en: 3- If sin causes stench, wounds and pains, then good works produce a sweet fragrance before God, the building up of the soul, spiritual growth, and rest of the body.

38.4.0.en: 6- I am twisted; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long.

38.4.1.en: 1- One of the effects of sin on David is that it made him twisted, so he was no longer standing erect in uprightness, glory and greatness, but became crooked, and it also made him writhe from its pains that squeeze his body and soul, and thus he felt the guilt of sin.

38.4.2.en: 2- David's twisting is the result of the fear and terror that sin caused him, whereas purity of heart gives strength, peace and uprightness.

38.4.3.en: 3- Sin also made David bow toward the ground in shame before God, so that he cannot lift up his head before Him, but is in shame and disgrace like the tax collector who could not lift up his eyes toward God, and bowed his head because of the shame of his sin (Lk 18:13).

38.4.4.en: 4- If the sin of adultery and murder carries behind it the sin of pride, after committing them David felt his evil, so he bowed toward the ground in repentance and seeking forgiveness, for pride is a lifting up, and repenting of it needs humility and looking to the ground. For God protects the humble from falling into sin.

38.4.5.en: 5- David's sins are lusts that he carried out; he acted carnally, looking to the earth and its lusts; therefore the result was that he bowed toward the dust of the earth, to know the result of his sin.

38.4.6.en: 6- Sin caused David exceedingly great grief, to the utmost, whereas virtue gives joy and peace.

38.4.7.en: 7- Man's twisting and bowing toward the ground, that is, his abasement and shame, continue all the day long, that is, throughout life, unless he repents, in which case God forgives him, lifts him up and glorifies him.

38.4.8.en: 8- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who said that His soul was sorrowful even unto death, and who fell "bowed down" to the ground under the weight of the Cross; all this Christ endured for our sins.

38.5.0.en: 7- For my loins are filled with burning, and there is no health in my flesh.

38.5.2.en: 1- One of the effects of sin is that David suffered hard pains in his loins, like one who suffers from severe renal colic, and by burning he means that they are pains beyond endurance. This shows:

38.5.4.en: B - The extent of David's remorse.

38.5.5.en: 2- David declares that his pains are hard and have no healing, "there is no health in my flesh," and the only solution is to return to God by repentance that He may remove his sin from him.

38.6.0.en: 8- I am benumbed and crushed to the utmost; I groaned from the sighing of my heart.

38.6.1.en: I am benumbed: I lost my feeling and grew weak.

38.6.2.en: 1- David was greatly affected when he fell into sin, so he lost his feeling toward God and his will was loosened, and he became like a person who has been anesthetized and become unconscious, and so rushed toward sin.

38.6.3.en: 2- Sin shattered David and crushed him, so he lost his spiritual being and his enjoyment of God's presence; his being crushed to the utmost means that he became like the dust of the earth, or the sand of the seas, or in the extreme of weakness, and lost his ability to walk in God's way, for here sin dominated him and he fell into it.

38.6.4.en: 3- David felt remorse after his fall, so he offered repentance not only with his lips but from all his heart, and sighed with a deep groan, which is expressed here by the sighing of the heart, that is, a continual groaning with every breath he breathes out. This made God grant him forgiveness.

38.7.0.en: 9- Lord, all my moaning is before thee; and my sighing is not hid from thee.

38.7.1.en: 1- Here David affirms his deep remorse by two things, which are:

38.7.2.en: A - Moaning, which is sounds coming out of his mouth.

38.7.3.en: B - Sighing, which is a groaning that comes out of his depths.

38.7.4.en: 2- David's moaning and sighing are before God, seeking His forgiveness, and not moaning and sighing between himself and his own self, because the latter produces despair, whereas the former is before God, and so establishes his hope in God's mercies and forgiveness.

38.7.5.en: 3- The moaning and sighing before God is prayer, and it is a prayer marked by the following:

38.7.6.en: A - A deep prayer with the heart and the tongue.

38.7.7.en: B - A continual prayer, because the sighing is continual.

38.7.8.en: And by this David offers a constant prayer full of hope, because it is offered to God who knows the secrets of hearts, and nothing is hidden from Him. And by these prayers David receives not only forgiveness but peace, and his heart is attached to God, and consequently keeps away from sin.

38.8.0.en: 10- My heart throbs; my strength hath left me, and the light of mine eyes also is not with me.

38.8.2.en: 1- When David fell into sin his heart was affected and shaken much, and its beats became rapid, because he did something foreign to his nature, which is sin, and also fell into disobedience to God, and the pleasure of lust turned into bitterness, pain and turmoil.

38.8.3.en: 2- David's rushing toward sin with force dropped him into extreme weakness, so he felt that his strength had left him, that is, God's strength working in him, because he was separated from God by sin, and became like one dead.

38.8.4.en: 3- Likewise by falling into sin David lost the light of his eyes, that is, his spiritual enlightenment and his ability to discern, because sin is error and spiritual blindness.

38.8.5.en: 4- David's feeling of all these effects of sin, and his confession of it, confirm his judging himself and his repentance, and consequently his receiving God's forgiveness.

38.9.0.en: 11- My loved ones and my friends stand opposite my stroke, and my relatives stand afar off. 12- And they that seek my soul set a snare, and they that seek my ill speak corruptions, and all the day long they mutter deceit.

38.9.1.en: 1- Sin is evil and troubles people; all the loved ones and friends who knew that David was a man of God were greatly troubled and kept away from him, because he had kept away from God. For the secret of David's strength, which made his loved ones gather around him, is his love for God.

38.9.2.en: 2- Sin destroys the close relationships of man, so even his relatives keep away from him. For sin is loathsome, and consequently it makes man lose the support of those around him, and he feels isolation; if he is a wise man he hastens to repent, and so feels God's support, and then his loved ones and his relatives return to him.

38.9.3.en: 3- David was surprised that his loved ones turned against him, and this was wounding to him. David had served King Saul by playing music for him when the unclean spirit came upon him, and Saul rose against him and tried to strike him with the spear several times (1 Sam 18:11). And David brought Ahithophel near to him as a counselor, and he turned against him and devised a plot to kill him, and even his son Absalom rose up against him and drove him out, and tried to kill him.

38.9.4.en: 4- This verse applies to Christ, who was left by all His loved ones at the hour of His arrest and in His sufferings, and He said "and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me" (Jn 16:32); His disciples scattered from Him, and His nation stood against Him when they tried Him and handed Him over to Pilate.

38.9.5.en: 5- When we commit sin we are scattered from Christ, and even stand against Him, though He is the Beloved who died for our salvation; thus we are turned from loved ones into enemies.

38.9.6.en: And when we commit sin our loved ones, the angels and the saints, are scattered from us. While when we repent of our sins, the friends of evil stand far from us.

38.9.7.en: 6- David was exposed not only to his loved ones' forsaking him, but to the enemies' rising against him, who wronged him with many evils, which are:

38.9.8.en: A - They tried to kill him, and set snares to catch him, as Saul, Absalom and Ahithophel did.

38.9.9.en: B - They spoke corruptions against David, and words of deceit and falsehood, as Shimei the son of Gera did, and all the followers of Saul.

38.9.10.en: 7- Christ was exposed to false testimonies from the Jews in His trial, in addition to false accusations, such as accusing Him of being a blasphemer, an evildoer, an agitator of the nation, and of cooperating with Beelzebub the prince of the demons.

38.9.11.en: Beware of the glitter of sin that tries to draw you, for it carries poison within it. Remember its pains and that it will destroy you, so repent and return from it, and from everything connected with it, whatever the cost, for your salvation is more important than anything. And rely on God and lean on Him, for He is able to give you victory and save you from it.

38.10.0.en: 13- But I am as a deaf man; I hear not, and as a dumb man who openeth not his mouth. 14- And I am like a man who heareth not, and in whose mouth is no argument.

38.10.1.en: 1- David heard many false, void accusations, but was not disturbed by them, but was like a deaf man who does not hear, that is, he kept his inward peace and the steadfastness of his faith, and even prayed for the one who wronged him.

38.10.2.en: 2- Likewise David did not answer the false accusations that Saul's servants raised against him, but only affirmed his love for Saul in practice, when Saul fell twice into his hand and David did not harm him. And David did not answer because he did not want to enter into useless argument; he speaks when there is benefit in his speaking, so he was like a dumb man, or one who has no argument although he is able to answer, but he speaks only at the proper time.

38.10.3.en: 3- What helped David in his silence was his occupation with his repentance, so he did not answer Shimei the son of Gera, and accepted his wrongs as though they were chastening from God (2 Sam 16:11, 12).

38.10.4.en: 4- Christ was completely silent before the accusations, the false testimonies and the useless discussions, whether from the scribes and Pharisees, or the chief priests during His trial, or before the civil rulers, such as Pilate and Herod.

38.11.0.en: 15- For in thee, O LORD, have I waited; thou wilt answer, O Lord my God. 16- For I said, lest they rejoice over me; when my foot slipped they magnified themselves against me.

38.11.1.en: 1- David was patient with the wrongs of his enemies and the forsaking of his loved ones, because he believed that God is a just judge and will not let his right be lost, so he endured for God's sake, and God lifted him up and glorified him on earth and in heaven, and this is evidence of David's firm hope in God.

38.11.2.en: 2- David's silence was accompanied by prayers that he trusted God would answer at the proper time, and this confirms David's faith in God's love, and in His ability to answer for him against the wrongs directed at him.

38.11.3.en: 3- And he asks God to intervene quickly so that his enemies do not gloat over him, for he is silent before their wrongs and accusations, waiting for God's intervention and defense of him, and this also confirms his hope in God.

38.11.4.en: 4- David's enemies, and even more the demons, exploited David's fall into the sin of adultery and murder, so they magnified themselves and were proud against him, exploiting his weakness; but he was wiser than they, for he humbled himself and took refuge in God by repentance, so He put his sin away from him and forgave him.

38.12.0.en: 17- For I am ready to halt, and my pain is continually before me.

38.12.2.en: 1- The slipping of David's foot - that is, his falling into sin - made him exposed to other falls and wars from the devil, so the slipping turns into constant weakness, that is, he keeps limping throughout his life, and what is meant is the continuation of his falling into sin.

38.12.3.en: And here David's humility appears, and his seeking God's help and His swift intervention to rescue him from the hand of Satan.

38.12.4.en: 2- David declares here that his pain - that is, his sin - is before his eyes at all times, and this means the following:

38.12.5.en: A - Constant remorse and contrition before God.

38.12.6.en: B - Constant guarding against sin so as not to fall into it a second time.

38.12.7.en: C - It confirms David's holding fast to the fear of God; for he feels the guilt of his sin before God's righteousness, and although he is confident that God has forgiven him, he thanks God at all times for His forgiveness.

38.12.8.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, who is ready to endure sufferings unto death to complete the salvation of mankind; Christ draws near to the crucifixion and says "I am ready to halt," that is, to be crucified, "and my pain is before me," that is, the sufferings of the crucifixion before His eyes. This confirms that Christ had a true body, and endured all the sufferings for us to redeem us.

38.13.0.en: 18- For I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin.

38.13.1.en: 1- David declares his confession of his sin before all peoples in this psalm, and this is great courage, because he is concerned for the salvation of his soul whatever the cost or disgrace.

38.13.2.en: 2- The cause of David's grief is his sin, which he remembers at all times, and not any affliction or punishment that comes upon him; repentance is his chief concern.

38.13.3.en: 3- David's repentance and confession of his sin are what enabled him to pray, asking God's help, and so he received His mercies.

38.14.0.en: 19- But mine enemies are living, and they are mighty: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied.

38.14.1.en: 1- David met a problem, which is that his wicked enemies were full of vitality and strength, and even grew great in their position, power, authority and wealth. All this did not affect David, because he held fast to his faith, confident of God's power that supports him. He was not troubled by their strength and greatness, because he believes in contentment and detachment, and did not doubt because of their greatness, because he is confident of God's power with him, and that God is able to compensate him with inward peace and joy better than all the delights and powers of the world.

38.14.2.en: 2- Among the problems that David met also was that his enemies who hate him and seek evil for him increased in number, but he did not doubt his faith and his conduct, even if he remained alone, but kept living in purity and love toward those who hate him, so he forgave Saul and did not harm him although he fell twice into David's hand. He is an example of steadfastness in the faith.

38.15.0.en: 20- And they that render evil for good are mine adversaries; because I follow the thing that good is.

38.15.1.en: 1- It is strange that a person should repay good with evil; for the natural man, not the spiritual, repays good with good and evil with evil, but the wicked alone is the one who repays good with evil. But David, who held fast to goodness, remained in his upright conduct, and did not answer evil with evil, but answered evil with good, so he did good to King Saul and did not harm him. Likewise he was tender toward his son Absalom, who drove him out and tried to kill him, and he used to say to his army going out to fight Absalom, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom" (2 Sam 18:5). He is an example of the love of enemies that Christ proclaimed in the New Testament, but David lived it in the Old Testament.

38.15.2.en: 2- The wicked repay good with evil, because the light of the righteous exposes the evil of the wicked, so instead of the wicked imitating the righteous and correcting their ways, they are enraged and wrong the righteous, to put out their light, that they may continue in their darkness.

38.15.3.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, who came for the salvation of the world, and went about everywhere doing good, and the Jews rose up against Him and crucified Him, and repaid His good with their evils, while He died for their salvation. It is the love that surpasses the mind.

38.16.0.en: 21- Forsake me not, O LORD my God: be not far from me. 22- Make haste to help me, O LORD my salvation.

38.16.1.en: 1- Before the strength of the enemies David took refuge in God with faith, asking Him not to forsake him, because he trusts in God's power that is able to protect him, declaring by this his need of God. He is truly a humble man.

38.16.2.en: 2- The psychological pressures that fell on David from the forsaking of friends and loved ones, and the rising of enemies against him, made him feel that only one support was left to him, which is God's being with him, and this is very sufficient and satisfying to him; therefore he urges God not to go far from him. And within God's embrace he is satisfied, rejoices and is strengthened.

38.16.3.en: 3- David's enemies had surrounded him and almost destroyed him, so he asks for swift help from God, and he feels boldness with God, so he says to Him, "O my God." And he asks for God's swift intervention and believes that God is his Savior; He will surely deliver him; therefore David lives at rest however much the enemies surround him.

38.16.4.en: 4- Though David fell into sin, and declared to us at the beginning of the psalm its results and its pains, yet when he looked to God and lifted his heart to Him, he was strengthened, empowered, and filled with peace and joy. The repentant prayer moves us from death to life, and from weakness to strength.

38.16.5.en: Give enough time to prayer, that you may enjoy your relationship with God, be rid of your sins by repentance, and lean on God in all your steps, and so live a calm life full of divine love.

38.16.6.en: A lament of a stranger. To the chief Musician. To Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. "I said, I will take heed to my way, that I err not" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

38.16.8.en: 2- Jeduthun led the singers with this psalm, and this Jeduthun is most likely Ethan the Ezrahite, who with Heman the Ezrahite was chief singers, assistants to Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David. The name Jeduthun is repeated in the title of Psalms 62 and 77.

38.16.10.en: A - Either in the days of David's flight from the face of Absalom.

38.16.11.en: B - Or during David's flight to the Philistine city of Gath to Achish its king.

38.16.12.en: 4- This psalm is considered a personal lament of David, in which he declares his labors and pains, and it is related to the psalm before it and the one after it. It is one of the greatest laments of David.

38.16.13.en: 5- This psalm is also full of hope and faith, so it is a help to those who pass through afflictions.

38.16.14.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
